analysis.one_liner: Caps Senate campaign spending, bans unlimited 'soft money' to party committees, and strengthens enforcement of campaign finance rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced July 23, 1997 by Senator Jack Reed with three Democratic cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Rules and Administration Committee until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a mandatory spending ceiling for Senate campaigns (roughly $1.18 million, higher in large states, adjusted for inflation), capped independent expenditures that support or attack candidates, banned national and state party committees from raising or spending unregulated 'soft money,' shut down 'leadership PACs' that senators use to bankroll other politicians, and given the Federal Election Commission stronger tools — random audits, injunctions, and bigger fines. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, by reducing the role of very large, loosely regulated donations in Senate elections. The bill's own findings say donors giving big money — less than 3 percent of the public — appeared to receive favored access to lawmakers, and that constant fundraising distracted senators from governing [S3]. Challengers to incumbents also gain, since the spending caps would have applied to 80 percent of incumbent Senate candidates in the last three elections but only 18 percent of challengers [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bans national and state party committees from soliciting, receiving, or spending 'soft money' — funds outside the contribution limits and disclosure rules of federal law — and bars federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting such funds [S2][S3].

Caps total Senate campaign spending at the greater of $1,182,500 or a formula based on state population, adjusted for inflation, with primary and runoff elections limited to shares of that total [S3].

Limits independent expenditures — spending by outside groups advocating a candidate's election or defeat — and treats coordinated spending as a contribution to the candidate, closing a major loophole [S2][S3].
Eliminates leadership PACs, the committees federal officeholders set up to collect and redistribute money beyond their own campaign limits, with existing PACs wound down within a year [S3].

Strengthens enforcement: the FEC could conduct random post-election audits, seek court injunctions when a violation is imminent, process complaints quickly near elections, and fine knowing violations up to $15,000 or triple the amount involved [S2][S3].

Prohibits campaign contributions from people not qualified to vote in federal elections and requires detailed reporting of 'issue advocacy' spending over $10,000 by non-party groups within 24–48 hours [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: National and state political party committees, which would lose soft money fundraising; wealthy donors and big-spending outside groups, whose unlimited expenditures would be capped or reported; federal officeholders whose leadership PACs would close; and broadcast media, which would sell fewer high-priced campaign ads. Candidates who currently outspend the proposed limits would have to operate under a ceiling.
analysis.who_pays_short: Party committees, big donors, outside spenders

drawbacks.text: The Supreme Court held in Buckley v. Valeo (1976) that mandatory campaign spending limits violate the First Amendment — a problem the bill's own findings acknowledge; the bill includes fallback rules that apply whenever the spending limits are not in effect, leaving the core caps on legally uncertain ground [S2][S3].

The bill raises individual contribution limits — allowing up to $30,000 per year in total contributions and $25,000 to candidates — and creates new 'State Party Grassroots Funds' that individuals can fund with up to $20,000 a year, channeling more money through party committees even as it bans soft money [S2][S3].

A hard spending cap can disadvantage a candidate facing a wealthy self-funding opponent or a flood of attack ads; the bill responds by allowing the cap to rise dollar-for-dollar when outside spending exceeds the limit, but that mechanism depends on quick FEC action and could be difficult in a fast-moving campaign [S3].

New definitions of coordination, express advocacy, and election activity would require more reporting and legal compliance from parties, candidates, and advocacy groups, raising the cost and legal risk of ordinary political activity [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: mandatory spending caps and a soft money ban would directly reduce the weight of concentrated money in Senate elections, at the cost of restricting political speech and resting on constitutional ground the Supreme Court had already rejected in Buckley v. Valeo. The bill anticipates both problems — it includes fallback rules for when the caps fail in court and escalation provisions for self-funded opponents — but the design is complex, and it partially offsets the restrictions by raising individual contribution limits and building new party fundraising channels. On balance it was aimed at reducing the influence of large donors and party soft money, with the burden falling on parties, big spenders, and incumbent fundraising machines.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the Campaign Spending Control Act of 1997 on July 23, 1997, joined by Senators Bryan, Hollings, and Johnson as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion action in the House [S5].

The bill would have gone far beyond contemporaneous proposals by imposing mandatory spending limits on Senate campaigns and capping independent expenditures, in addition to banning soft money [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National and state party committees that raised soft money, wealthy donors and outside groups that spent without limits, and officeholders with leadership PACs — all kept the existing rules because the bill never advanced. Ordinary voters gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors, party soft-money operations, incumbents' PACs

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Sens. Richard Bryan, Ernest Hollings, and Tim Johnson

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no votes were ever taken; the bill died quietly in committee rather than being voted down, so the record shows no opposition votes, only the absence of action by the committee then chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill would ban the parties' soft money fundraising — contributions from corporations, unions, and large donors outside federal limits — and require federal-election activity to be paid for with regulated funds. Soft money had become a major channel for unlimited money into federal elections.

industries.industry: Wealthy donors and large outside spenders
industries.note: Caps on independent expenditures, bans on contributions from people not qualified to vote, and disclosure of issue-advocacy spending over $10,000 would directly limit how much and how freely large donors could spend. The bill's findings note big donors made up less than 3 percent of the public yet appeared to receive favored access.

Spending caps for Senate campaigns and limits on independent and party expenditures would reduce the volume of high-priced campaign advertising, a major revenue source for television stations and media buyers.

industries.industry: Federal officeholders and their fundraising operations
industries.note: The bill would abolish leadership PACs, cutting off a fundraising channel incumbents use to bankroll colleagues and build influence, and the spending caps would have applied to 80 percent of incumbent Senate candidates in recent elections. At the same time, it raises individual contribution limits, easing fundraising within the new rules.
